summary: This document is one of a set describing the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), a successor to the old WHOIS protocol. It describes how RDAP is carried over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). RDAP has an internet-standard status.

eli5.summary: WHOIS is an old way to look up who owns a domain or address. This part explains how its modern replacement asks and answers over ordinary web connections.

questions: what http status codes does rdap use
what is the difference between rdap and whois
subtitle: How RDAP, the modern replacement for WHOIS, uses plain HTTP to ask for and return registration data.

tldr.problem: WHOIS is a very old protocol that is insufficient for modern registration data needs such as redirection to authoritative sources, internationalized domain names and localized data.
tldr.mechanism: RDAP clients send an ordinary HTTP GET with an Accept header for a JSON media type. Servers answer with 200 for data, 3xx to point elsewhere, 404 for no data, 4xx for policy refusals and 400 for malformed queries.
tldr.outcome: A single simple client can query many different registration directories in the same way. The RFC is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7480 is an Internet Standard and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the HTTP profile for RDAP, alongside RFC 7481, RFC 7482, RFC 7483 and RFC 7484.

sections.title: Why RDAP Uses HTTP
sections.content:
RFC 7480 is one of a collection of documents that together describe the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), a successor to the very old WHOIS protocol. Registration data here means the records for domain names and Internet number resources. WHOIS services usually provide it, but the RFC says WHOIS is insufficient for modern requirements.

A replacement is expected to keep the simple transactional nature of WHOIS while adding a specification for queries and responses, redirection to authoritative sources, support for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and support for localized data such as addresses and names.

This document does not redefine HTTP. It ties together usage patterns of standard HTTP into one common profile, informed by the REST architectural style, so that a single client can retrieve data from many directory services that follow the same behavior.
sections.eli5: Old registration lookups were like many shops that each wanted you to ask in a different way. RDAP says everyone should use the normal web way of asking, so one visitor can shop anywhere.

sections.title: Design Intents
sections.content:
The RFC states three design criteria. First, each query should need only one path of execution: a response contains an answer, no answer or a redirect, and clients are not expected to fork multiple paths to make a query.

Second, the request and response semantics leave room for future and non-standard response formats. This document only notes a JSON response media type and leaves the contents to RFC 7483.

Third, the protocol is meant to use the range of HTTP mechanisms, such as cache control, authorization, compression and redirection, according to each operator's local policy. Where complexity has to live, the goal is to put it on the server and keep the client as simple as possible. A client should be possible with common scripting tools such as bash and wget.
sections.eli5: The rule is that the helper at the desk does the hard thinking, so the person asking only needs to ask once and follow one direction.

sections.title: Making a Query
sections.content:
The basic pattern has several steps. A client first works out which server and base URL to use; RFC 7484 describes one method. It then issues an HTTP or HTTPS query using GET, for example http://example.com/rdap/ip/192.0.2.0. The query formats themselves are in RFC 7482.

Clients use GET to retrieve a response body and HEAD to check whether data exists. Servers are under no obligation to support other methods. Clients and servers MUST support HTTPS.

To ask for an RDAP answer, the client includes an Accept header with an RDAP-specific JSON media type, the generic JSON media type, or both. The server returns an entity with a Content-Type naming the RDAP-specific JSON type. What a server does for any other or missing Accept value is not defined.

Servers MUST ignore unknown query parameters.
sections.eli5: You ask in the normal web way and say you want the answer in RDAP's data format. If the helper does not understand an extra word you added, it just ignores that word.

sections.title: Response Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines the minimal set of response codes a client needs to understand. No standard HTTP code is forbidden, and a robust client that handles these will give a better experience.

  • 200 (OK): the server has the information and returns it in the body.
  • 301, 302, 303, 307: the answer is elsewhere. 301 is permanent; the others are non-permanent. The Location header carries a complete HTTP(S) URL, which the client follows without transforming it.
  • 404 (Not Found): an empty result set. The server may add detail in the body.
  • 4xx: information exists but cannot be given for policy reasons. A client may retry if that suits the code.
  • 400 (Bad Request): the server cannot interpret the query as RDAP.
  • 429 (Too Many Requests): a rate limit applies.

A client that gets a 429 SHOULD decrease its query rate and honor Retry-After if present. The RFC notes this is not a defense against denial-of-service attacks, since a malicious client could ignore the code, and a server may choose another code if it does not want to reveal that rate limiting is the reason.
sections.eli5: The answers are like a shop assistant saying: here it is, try the shop next door, we do not have that, I cannot tell you, I did not understand, or please slow down.

sections.title: Redirects and Bootstrapping
sections.content:
A server that does not hold the data but knows who does can send a redirect. For example, a TLD operator might tell a client that the information it wants is held by another TLD operator. The server hands back a complete URL: if a client queried http://serv1.example.com/weirds/domain/example.com and the server redirects to https://serv2.example.net/weirds2/, the Location value is https://serv2.example.net/weirds2/domain/example.com.

Appendix C explains that WHOIS has no way to find the authoritative source; earlier approaches such as Joint WHOIS relied on proxies and server-side referrals. RDAP solves this with HTTP redirects and bootstrapping, discussed in RFC 7484. In constrained environments a server can act as a redirector, issuing redirects from a table informed by RFC 7484. Where networks have been sub-delegated between Regional Internet Registries or transferred, several redirects in a row can happen.
sections.eli5: If you ask the wrong office, the clerk gives you the full address of the right one. Sometimes you are passed along more than once before you arrive.

sections.title: Extensibility and Internationalization
sections.content:
The RFC defines an IANA registry of extension identifiers, used as prefixes in JSON names and in URL path segments. Identifiers SHOULD use only letters A to Z in either case, digits and the underscore, and SHOULD NOT begin with an underscore, a digit or the characters xml. The ABNF is name = ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" ). The reasons given are easy mapping to object attributes in languages such as Ruby or Java, and a clean mapping between JSON and XML.

The registry policy is Specification Required, so values and their meanings must be documented in a permanent and readily available reference.

For internationalization, clients may use IRIs internally but MUST convert them to URIs when talking to servers, and servers MUST use URIs in all responses. Servers SHOULD label data with language identifiers when known, and SHOULD ignore the Accept-Language header so clients do not confuse it with the lang values in the body. Servers MAY return a Content-Language header.
sections.eli5: New add-on features must have a unique name tag so they never clash, and names are kept to simple letters and digits. Web addresses must be written in the standard plain way, and answers are labeled with their language.

sections.title: Security and CORS
sections.content:
This document sets no strong security requirements of its own but does not restrict the use of HTTP security mechanisms. It does require that RDAP clients and servers MUST support HTTPS. Further security considerations are in RFC 7481.

For browser-based clients, servers are RECOMMENDED to send the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. A wildcard value (an asterisk) suits public resources. This lifts the same-origin restriction so a browser can load RDAP client code from one web server and query others. Using Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to send cookies is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Appendix B also describes cache busting: because some caches keep responses too long, a client may add an improbable unknown query parameter with a random value. This is not part of any specification and is offered for information only.
sections.eli5: Everyone must be able to talk over the locked, secure web connection. A special label also lets web pages ask other sites for public information safely.

viz.caption: RESPONSE CODES RDAP CLIENTS NEED TO UNDERSTAND

items.label: OK
items.desc: The answer is in the response body.

items.label: Bad Request
items.desc: The query cannot be interpreted as RDAP.

items.label: Too Many Requests
items.desc: Rate limit applied; slow down and honor Retry-After.
